cells.tense: You are in the practice now, and the practice is right here with you.
cells.ask: Break your own method on purpose once, then write the one part you would not change, and take that forward.
cells.core:
You keep showing up to it. Not the one who talks about it and not the one who waits for the mood — you decided this matters and you keep deciding it, so the thing has depth and not just heat.

What wears it thin is holding the method harder than the work needs. A deadline, a doubt, a rough week, and the rigor tightens into gripping; the fixing starts and the attention underneath gets lost. That attention is the part that has to survive. It is the thing that lets the method be wrong for a day without falling apart. When the grip loosens, the practice keeps going and the small light keeps burning. What you make stays yours because you stayed with it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the small practice lit, and it is yours.
cells.verb: holding to a method long enough that it tells you the thing
cells.place: where a small practice gets kept by attention and repetition

cells.tense: You are already at a result that has not arrived and cannot be forced.
cells.ask: Do one session and stop the moment a pass is done — mark it done out loud and do not touch it again until tomorrow.
cells.core:
You are running ahead of the work. Before a pass is finished you are back in it, testing and sharpening the next version, and the practice has turned into a strain instead of the answer to one. Pushing like this costs you what you push toward.

Somewhere ahead there is a version where the method finally holds. You are living in that version already, so every session is a chance to close the gap. But the tightening shows up in the hands and the breath. Solitude here was meant to connect, not to disappear into the next revision. When you let one pass stand, the work gets stronger and the light stays clean. The way back is to admit a thing is done and let it be done.
cells.sheetLine: Polishing has taken the place of practicing.

cells.tense: You have stepped back from the practice and you still stand at that door.
cells.ask: Do the practice once this week for someone else — five minutes, badly if it goes badly — and let their response be the only score you keep.
cells.core:
There is a practice here you do not practice. The set-up is right; the hands do not move. What is missing is not effort or a better method. Nobody is in the room with you, so the time goes unanswered, and unanswered work fades out.

Solitude was supposed to be a place you connect from, not a place you vanish into. Adding more force to a cold room only makes it colder. Give one small piece of it away this week and let their reply tell you what is there. Five minutes, badly, in front of one person, and the work starts to move again on its own. The exchange does what effort will not, and the door you are standing at opens from the other side.

cells.tense: You are already running the method and calling it the pressure of the situation.
cells.ask: Say one thing you have been doing to a piece of work: 'This is mine.' Write the sentence down and keep it.
cells.core:
You already rule how this gets done. Not because a title says so, but because you have done the work, and it sets the pace and the order of what comes next. You describe it as if the task ran that way on its own. The steering is real; the admitting is not.

The practice is yours. You set the standard without announcing it, and the people near the work adjust to it. When that stays unnamed, your discipline looks like the situation rather than a choice you made, and the choice goes uncounted. Name one moment this week, out loud, once. The bridge under this practice gets solid again and the small light steadies. Saying it costs nothing and returns the work to you.
cells.sheetLine: You already set the standard. You have not owned it out loud.
